script.opening: “Hi, sorry to bother you. My baby Freya is five days old and she looks a bit yellow — more than when the midwife came. And she’s really sleepy. Is that normal? The midwife’s not due till tomorrow.”

facts.text: “The midwife said her face was a bit yellow on Tuesday — that was day three. I didn’t notice it on the first day in hospital. Today it’s her tummy and her legs, and the whites of her eyes look yellow.”
If asked to press gently on her nose or chest and look at the skin colour in daylight: “Yes, it’s yellow underneath when I press. And her gums look yellowish.”
“I have to wake her for feeds. She opens her eyes and looks at me, then goes back to sleep. She’s not floppy — she grips my finger.” Cry: “normal, not high-pitched.” No arching or stiffness.
“Breastfeeding. She feeds maybe six or seven times a day, but only for five minutes and then she falls asleep. My milk came in yesterday I think. It hurts — my nipples are cracked.”
“Three wet nappies yesterday. Poos are mustard yellow and seedy. Her wee is pale, not dark.”
“I haven’t got a thermometer. She doesn’t feel hot.” No rash, no vomiting (only small possets), breathing normal.

“She was born at 38 weeks and 5 days. Normal delivery. They did a vitamin K injection. They didn’t say she needed any treatment.” Mother’s blood group: “O positive, I think.” No sibling with jaundice (first baby).
“The midwife said she’d lost about 8% on Tuesday.”
“My partner, Jack, went back to work today. My mum lives in Spain. I don’t drive.”
If asked how she is: “I’m okay… I’m just tired. I cried a lot today.” If asked about thoughts of harming herself or the baby: “No, nothing like that — I’m just exhausted.”
If asked how feeding is going for her, or what she thinks has caused the jaundice: “I think I’m starving her. My milk’s not enough. Will they make me give her formula? I really want to breastfeed.”

Apologetic and tired, voice shaky. Answer clearly when asked specific questions. If told Freya needs checking today, ask “Can’t it wait for the midwife tomorrow?” once, then accept if the reason is explained. Become tearful when feeding is discussed. If the doctor is kind about breastfeeding, open up about the cracked nipples and feeling alone. If they say “just give formula”, go quiet.

ice.ideas: “Maybe it’s normal newborn jaundice — or maybe I’m not feeding her enough.”
ice.concerns: That she is starving her baby; that she will be made to stop breastfeeding; being on her own.
ice.expectations: Reassurance, or advice to wait for the midwife tomorrow.

cues: “Sorry to bother you” — she feels she is overreacting.
“Jack went back to work today” — alone, low support.

checkpoints.text: Establishes age at onset, current extent of jaundice and eye involvement, and checks there was no jaundice in the first 24 hours
Assesses feeding, wet and dirty nappies, alertness, tone, cry and temperature, and asks about stool and urine colour (pale stools or dark urine)
Identifies risk factors — gestation, exclusive breastfeeding, weight loss, sibling with jaundice, blood group
Arranges bilirubin measurement within 6 hours through the local pathway (same-day midwife/neonatal assessment) rather than waiting for tomorrow’s visit
Gives clear danger signs needing 999 or ED (very hard to wake, floppy, high-pitched cry, arching, fever, not feeding) and how to get there
Supports breastfeeding — frequent feeds at least 8–12 times a day, help with latch and sore nipples, infant feeding team — and does not advise stopping breastfeeding
Responds to the mother’s fear of “starving her”, validates the call, and checks her mood and support
Explains jaundice in plain language and why a blood test today matters, and checks understanding

worked.txt: “You’re not bothering me at all — you were right to ring.”
“Where can you see the yellow now — face, tummy, legs? Are the whites of her eyes yellow?”
“What colour are her poos and her wee? Mustard yellow poo is good; pale or chalky poo or dark wee would need a different check.”
“Jaundice is very common at this age, but because she’s more yellow and very sleepy and not feeding well, she needs her jaundice level measured today — within the next few hours, not tomorrow.”
“This isn’t your fault and it doesn’t mean you have to stop breastfeeding. Feeding more often helps her clear the jaundice. The infant feeding team can help with your latch and sore nipples.”
“How are you doing yourself, with Jack back at work?”

f.learning: Most newborn jaundice is physiological, but every baby with visible jaundice needs a bilirubin level: within 2 hours if jaundice appears in the first 24 hours, and within 6 hours if it is noticed after 24 hours. Do not rely on visual inspection to estimate the level, particularly in darker skin. Sleepiness and poor feeding are both a cause and a consequence of rising bilirubin. Always ask about stool and urine colour: pale chalky stools or dark urine suggest conjugated jaundice (for example biliary atresia) and need urgent specialist referral. Prolonged jaundice is beyond 14 days in term babies (21 in preterm). Encourage frequent breastfeeding and arrange skilled support rather than advising formula or water; check the mother’s mood and support.

wordPics.clearPass: Takes a focused, structured phone history including stool and urine colour and danger signs, recognises the need for bilirubin within 6 hours and arranges it directly that day, supports breastfeeding and the mother’s wellbeing warmly, and gives clear, specific escalation advice.
wordPics.pass: Arranges same-day assessment with bilirubin and gives reasonable safety-netting; feeding or maternal mood addressed more briefly.
wordPics.fail: Recognises jaundice but defers to tomorrow’s midwife visit, or advises sunlight/formula without a bilirubin measurement; misses stool colour.
wordPics.clearFail: Reassures that newborn jaundice is normal with no measurement or safety-net, or advises stopping breastfeeding; does not ask about alertness or feeding.

avoid.dont: “Put her near a sunny window — that helps the jaundice.”
avoid.instead: “She needs her level measured today; that tells us if she needs treatment like phototherapy.”
avoid.why: Sunlight is not a treatment and delays measurement.

avoid.dont: “Top her up with formula or water.”
avoid.instead: “Feed her more often — at least 8 to 12 times a day — and let’s get you some help with feeding.”
avoid.why: Undermines breastfeeding; water is not recommended for jaundice.

avoid.instead: “This needs checking today, within the next few hours.”
avoid.why: Visible jaundice after 24 hours needs bilirubin within 6 hours.

model.text: Hello Chloe, it’s Dr Okoro calling back about Freya. Tell me what you’ve noticed.
Sorry to bother you. She looks more yellow than when the midwife came, and she’s really sleepy.
You’re not bothering me — you did the right thing ringing. When did you first notice the yellow? Was it there on her first day?
No, the midwife saw it on day three, on her face. Now it’s her tummy and legs and her eyes.
How is she feeding — how often and for how long? And how many wet nappies yesterday?
Six or seven times, only five minutes and she falls asleep. Three wet nappies.
What colour are her poos and her wee?
Poos are mustard yellow. Wee is pale.
That’s helpful. When you wake her, does she open her eyes and look at you? Is she floppy, or crying in a high-pitched way, or arching her back? Does she feel hot?
She looks at me then goes back to sleep. She grips my finger. Normal cry. She doesn’t feel hot.

Jaundice is very common in the first week, but because it’s spreading and she’s sleepy and not feeding well, she needs her jaundice level measured today — within the next few hours. I’ll arrange this now with the midwives and the hospital team.
model.why: Clear decision in line with the 6-hour rule

model.text: Can’t it wait for the midwife tomorrow?

I understand it’s hard on your own. Most babies just need a quick skin or heel-prick test and some don’t need treatment, but if the level is high, light treatment works well and it’s better to start early.
(crying) I think I’m starving her. Will they make me give her formula?

This isn’t your fault, and it doesn’t mean you have to stop breastfeeding. Feeding often — at least 8 to 12 times a day, waking her if needed — helps her clear the jaundice, and the infant feeding team can help with your latch and sore nipples.
And how are you, with Jack back at work today? How is your mood?
Exhausted. I’ve cried a lot. Nothing more than that.

The midwife team or hospital will phone you within the hour with where to go; I’ll call you back if you haven’t heard. Can Jack come home to take you? If before then she becomes very hard to wake, floppy, has a high-pitched cry, arches her back, feels hot or won’t feed at all, call 999. What will you do now?
model.why: Follow-up, transport and specific escalation with teach-back

model.text: Wait for their call, ring Jack, and 999 if she’s floppy or won’t wake.

knowledge.guideline: NICE CG98 Jaundice in newborn babies under 28 days (2010, updated 2023) · NICE NG194 Postnatal care (2021) · UNICEF UK Baby Friendly Initiative standards
knowledge.summary: Visible jaundice in a baby over 24 hours old needs a bilirubin measurement within 6 hours; within 2 hours if under 24 hours old. Do not estimate the level by eye. Check stool and urine colour for conjugated jaundice. Support breastfeeding.

points.t: Jaundice in the first 24 hours: measure serum bilirubin urgently (within 2 hours). After 24 hours: measure bilirubin within 6 hours of suspicion, using a transcutaneous meter if 35 weeks or more and over 24 hours old.
Examine in good natural light, blanching the skin and checking sclerae and gums. Visual inspection underestimates jaundice, especially in darker skin tones.
Gestation under 38 weeks, previous sibling needing phototherapy, exclusive breastfeeding, visible jaundice in the first 24 hours, significant weight loss.
Very sleepy and hard to wake, floppy, high-pitched cry, arching, fever, poor or no feeding — urgent same-day medical review or 999.
Pale chalky stools and/or dark urine that stains the nappy suggest conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia (for example biliary atresia): urgent specialist referral and split bilirubin.

Jaundice beyond 14 days (term) or 21 days (preterm): measure total and conjugated bilirubin, FBC, blood group and DAT, consider urine culture if infection suspected, and check thyroid screening result.
Encourage frequent breastfeeds; do not routinely give water or dextrose. Arrange skilled feeding support. Phototherapy decisions use treatment threshold charts.
Ask about mood, sleep and support; postnatal low mood is common and may affect feeding.

social.t: First-time mother alone, partner back at work, no car: plan transport and support.

legal.t: Mother has parental responsibility; record who you spoke to and the advice given.

professional.t: Babies under 28 days are usually under community midwifery care; use the local jaundice pathway and hand over directly.

community.t: National Breastfeeding Helpline 0300 100 0212; local infant feeding team; NCT; health visitor.

redFlags: Very sleepy, floppy, high-pitched cry, arching
ice: Concern: starving her; being made to give formula
Expectation: reassurance or wait for midwife

playbook.diagnosis: Visible jaundice on day 5 extending to the legs, with sleepiness and poor feeding in an exclusively breastfed baby — needs bilirubin measurement within 6 hours.
playbook.diagnosisLay: “Jaundice happens when a yellow substance called bilirubin builds up because a baby’s liver is still getting going. It’s common, but we need to measure the level today to see if she needs light treatment.”

management.reflectIce: “You’re worried you’re starving her. Feeding more often will help, and you can keep breastfeeding — we’ll get you help with it.”
management.psychosocial: Arrange transport (partner); infant feeding support; ask about mood; health visitor follow-up.
sharedPlan: Same-day bilirubin via local midwife/neonatal pathway
Feed 8–12 times a day, wake if needed
safetyNet: 999/ED: hard to wake, floppy, high-pitched cry, arching, fever, not feeding
GP call-back if no contact within the hour

pitfalls.intro: The midwife is coming tomorrow; the mother would accept waiting. The baby needs a level today.

items.fail: Deferring to the next routine midwife visit.
items.why: Visible jaundice after 24 hours needs a bilirubin within 6 hours, and she is sleepy and feeding poorly.
items.fix: Arrange same-day measurement through the local pathway.

items.fail: Not asking about stool and urine colour.
items.why: Pale stools or dark urine point to conjugated jaundice, a different and urgent pathway.

items.fail: Advising formula top-ups or water as the plan.
items.why: Undermines breastfeeding; water does not help jaundice.
items.fix: More frequent breastfeeds and skilled support.

items.fail: Ignoring the tears and the isolation.
items.why: Maternal wellbeing affects feeding and safety.
items.fix: Ask how she is and who can help today.

cm.d: Tailored the plan to the patient’s circumstances, beliefs and practical barriers rather than giving a generic plan.

cm.t: Shares risks and safety of options

Moved efficiently through the consultation so all key areas were covered within the time without getting stuck.

ro.d: Follows “sorry to bother you”, “it hurts” about feeding and “Jack went back to work today”.
Idea (normal jaundice, or not feeding enough); concern (starving her, being made to stop breastfeeding, being alone); expectation (reassurance or wait for the midwife).
Warm, non-judgmental tone; put the patient at ease and showed respect for their perspective.
Opened broadly and let the patient tell their story before narrowing down.
When a cue was offered, stopped and explored the specific concern rather than reassuring superficially and moving on.
Active listening throughout — reflecting, pausing, not interrupting — interested in the patient as a person.
Told the patient why a question, examination or test was being done — transparent reasoning throughout.
Explained the working diagnosis or analysis in plain language the patient could understand.

ro.t: Shares and uses ICE in the plan
ro.d: Addressed the patient’s specific concern — That she is starving her baby; that she will be made to stop breastfeeding; being on her own — directly within the plan, rather than noting it and moving on.
Checked understanding, offered written/follow-up support, asked if anything else was on their mind, agreed next steps.
Clear agenda set early, logical flow from data gathering to management. Did not jump to a plan before gathering enough information.
Explained clinical terms in plain English, or defined them immediately; checked the patient was following.
Noticed and responded to emotional and verbal cues rather than continuing a fixed clinical script.
